title: Making images from space more accessible

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A curious twist of the advertising adage 'Image is everything’ emerged following the landing of the European Space Agencys (ESA) probe Huygens on Titan, Saturn's largest moon. Launched from the Cassini spacecraft already in orbit around Saturn, the Huygens probe beamed the first unprocessed images of Titans surface to Earth, via the Cassini spacecraft. The images thrilled scientists, but barely inspired most of the public. Yet, thanks to a few enthusiastic amateurs who have developed the expertise to interpret and reformat information from the raw images, awesome pictures of Titan were available on the internet within hours of the release.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scientists had meant to publish the raw images but, according to the ESA Huygens project manager, Jean-Pierre Lebreton, not quite so quickly. Apparently the University of Arizona server onto which the information from Huygens's cameras was uploaded was 'made accessible [to the public] by mistake’. The Huygens images were therefore available before the scientists had a chance to even look them over. And the public was waiting Not the general pub often show little interest in space exploration, but an informal group of amateur astronomers whose passion is for enhancing images from space. They convene via internet chat rooms and showcase pictures on personal web pages. One of these websites is run by Anthony Liekens, a doctoral student in biomedical imaging at the University of Eindhoven in the Netherlands.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Liekens's chat group was anticipating the Huygens data after they read a University of Arizona announcement that raw pictures would be available soon after the landing. But events unfolded much faster than even Liekens expected. After using the unprocessed information to compile mosaics of Titan’s surface, his group converted these from two-dimensional monochrome to three-dimensional color to provide an impression of Titan's surface using standard image-manipulation software such as Photoshop and Terragan The topography of the published results resembled serene landscapes complete with coastlines and islands, based on actual data but colored with the use of guesswork. This scenery was instantly recognizable to the human eye, even if the images lacked total accuracy. However, Liekens himself pointed out that the professionals are est equipped to render the most realistic views, as they have the expertise to interpret nonvisual data that may provide clues to features not evident from the raw pictures.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There seem to be no hard feelings between the amateurs and professionals. Lebreton says the amateurs should be given credit for clearly stating up front that their embellishments were not necessarily accurate, but meant to be enjoyed for what they represented. In fact, he says that ESA is looking to hire some of the amateurs who worked on the images. Lebreton thinks that the release of raw data has been an unexpected public relations success. The implications for future public relations go far beyond the ESA offices, and new technology may well dramatically change the amateur-professional interaction in the future.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Astronomy has long been a favorite discipline of amateur scientists, and amateur astronomers are often the first to detect comets or supernovae. For this reason, professional astronomers tend to value the contributions of amateurs.' Generally, the attitude [toward amateurs] is positive’, says Robert Milkey, executive officer of the American Astronomy Society. ‘Many professionals are eager to collaborate… The distinction between professionals and the best-qualified amateurs is that the professional is paid.' Ed Flaspoehler, president of the American Amateur Astronomical Association, perceives the professional community differently, as 'generally diffident toward amateurs.’ He says, 'Some professionals view amateurs as a pool of graduate students who do the work while [the professionals get the credit. Professionals have not yet figured how best to put this [resource] to good use’.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even if only a small proportion of the estimated 250,000 amateurs in the US want involvement at a higher level, Flaspoehler noted, that’s still a large number compared to the six or seven thousand professionals. New approaches make it possible for greater numbers of amateurs to be involved.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Milkey thinks that the technology [now] coming into the hands of amateurs is capable of doing serious science. 'Flaspoehler sees the Huygens imaging chat group as the latest trend in an evolutionary process. Early amateurs made visual observations, then graduated to telescopes In the 1980s, amateurs widely adapted film as a recording medium. During the 1990s, the technology in widespread use among observatories became affordable to amateurs in the form of digital cameras. Over the past few years, amateurs have adapted readily available digital cameras to take astronomical photographs and therefore become involved in image processing.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: ‘There’s a real need for organizations to bring amateurs and professionals together,’Robert Milkey remarked. He hopes that this would enable more members of the public to understand what keeps scientists coming to the observatory or laboratory every day- and give them the chance to participate in scientific research and experience that thrill for themselves.
